_readme: Country-level detail for the three compositions, applied by scripts/build_entities.py after the roll-ups. Each row names one country and one field. A row with 'groups' replaces the field with a census's own division of it and is always preferred -- or, where the census does not ask, a survey's, whose 'basis' says it is a survey estimate; a row with only a 'note' says what a large residual holds and why it is not divided. Neither invents a split. This is the admin-0 counterpart of admin1_seed.json, and it is curated for the same reason: adapter output lands on admin1 and admin2 shapes, and the country record is the Factbook profile plus whatever its children roll up into it.

rows.source: Uganda Bureau of Statistics, National Population and Housing Census 2014 -- Main Report, Appendix Table A8 (Population by Ethnicity/Citizenship by Sex and Residence)
rows.license: Uganda Bureau of Statistics; official statistics
rows.note: Uganda's 2014 census asks one question and takes two kinds of answer: a Ugandan names an ethnic group, a non-Ugandan a country of citizenship. This is Appendix Table A8 of the Main Report in full -- the sixty-five ethnic groups it names and its own 'Other Ugandans', each as a share of the 34,142,417 people it enumerates, with the 504,196 non-Ugandans pooled into one row rather than shown as eighteen more ethnic groups, which they are not. It replaces nine names and an 'other' of 32.1%, which were the same census's figures on a Ugandans-only base: that thirty-two per cent was the fifty-six groups the short list did not reach. The shares here are a per cent or so lower than the familiar ones because the base is everybody enumerated rather than Ugandans alone -- Baganda are 16.5% of Ugandans and 16.3% of the country.

rows.source: Vanuatu Bureau of Statistics and the Pacific Community, Vanuatu 2020 National Population and Housing Census -- Analytical Report Volume 2
rows.license: SPC and VBoS; reproduction permitted for research with acknowledgement
rows.note: The 82.6% is first language spoken, from the 2020 census, and it is not one language: Vanuatu has more than a hundred, the highest number of languages per head of population anywhere on earth, all of them Oceanic languages of the Austronesian family. None of them is large. The biggest -- Lenakel and Whitesands on Tanna, Apma and Raga on Pentecost, the languages of north Efate and of Ambrym -- are counted in the thousands, so not one of them reaches five per cent of the country. The census records which language each person first spoke and the Bureau publishes none of them: the 2020 Analytical Report carries the four-way split alone -- indigenous language, Bislama, English, French -- and treats 'Indigenous language' as a single category throughout. The individual codes exist in the microdata and in nothing published. Dividing the column here would mean dividing it by speaker estimates of mixed vintage, most of them counts made around 2000 for a country that has grown by three-fifths since, and that would be this project's arithmetic wearing the census's clothes.

rows.source: US Department of State, 2021 Report on International Religious Freedom: Bahrain, reading Bahrain's 2020 census
rows.license: Public domain (U.S. Government work)
rows.note: Bahrain's census asks religion and publishes the answer as two numbers: Muslim, and not. The 25.9% is the whole of the not, and it is almost entirely the foreign residents who are about half of everybody living in the country. Reading the same 2020 census, the US State Department's religious freedom report puts roughly 401,500 foreign residents as Muslim and roughly 387,800 as Hindu, Buddhist, Baha'i, Sikh or Christian -- the Christians chiefly Roman Catholic, Protestant, Syrian Orthodox and Mar Thoma, from south India -- and that is as far as any published figure divides this column. Bahraini citizens are about 99.8% Muslim by the Ministry of Information's own count, so hardly any of it is theirs. No count of Hindus, of Christians, or of the few dozen Bahraini Jews is published, so none is shown.

The 32.4% is everything that is not Spanish, and the Factbook's own line names what is in it: Fang, Bubi, the two other official languages Portuguese and French, and the Fa d'Ambo of Annobon -- to which belong Ndowe, Benga, Bisio and the Pichinglis of Bioko. Read it as a measure of Spanish rather than of anyone's mother tongue: Spanish is the language of school, government and the towns and is a second language for most of the people counted in it. The figure is a 1994 estimate and nothing has replaced it. The nearest thing to a division of the column is the ethnicity row on this same record, which is the 2011 census -- Fang 78.1%, Bubi 9.4%, Ndowe 2.8%, Bisio 0.9% -- each of those a people whose language carries the same name.

The ten names above are Ghana's largest ethnolinguistic groups in the 2010 census, and several are divisions of one larger group: Asante, Fante, Akyem and Boron are all Akan, and Dagomba and Dagarte are both Mole-Dagbani. The 31.2% is the rest of the same two clusters -- Akuapem, Kwahu, Nzema, Sefwi, Wassa and Aowin among the Akan, Mamprusi, Nanumba, Wali and Frafra among the Mole-Dagbani -- together with the Gurma, Guan, Grusi and Mande languages and Hausa. The census divides the same people into those eight clusters and leaves only 1.6% over: Akan 45.7%, Mole-Dagbani 18.5%, Ewe 12.8%, Ga-Dangme 7.1%, Gurma 6.4%, Guan 3.2%, Grusi 2.7%, Mande 2.0% (2021 census). What it does not publish is a division of the language question itself, so the column is left as it stands rather than being given the ethnicity table's shape.

rows.source: INE Bolivia, Censo de Población y Vivienda 2024, person database (summed from the nine departments)
rows.license: INE Bolivia; official statistics
rows.note: Question 32 of the 2024 census, put to everyone of every age: whether a person identifies with a nación o pueblo indígena originario campesino or as Afro-Bolivian, and if so which, grouped as INE groups the answers. Counted from INE's person database, the 11,124,437 of 11,365,333 people enumerated who answered, summed from the nine departments. Those who answered no are the remainder: the census asks nothing about mestizo or white identity. It replaces the Factbook's line (Mestizo 68%, Indigenous 20%, White 5%), which is not a census count; the country's divisions are not summed automatically because the Factbook's 2025 population estimate (12.4 million) is 9% above the census count (11,365,333).

Counted from INE's 2024 person database, summed from the nine departments. It replaces the Factbook's line (Spanish 68.1%, Quechua 17.2%, Aymara 10.5%).

rows.source: National Statistics Office of Mongolia, 2020 Population and Housing Census of Mongolia: National Report (English edition), Table 3.2: population and ethnic groups, 2010, 2020
rows.license: Official statistics of the National Statistics Office of Mongolia, cited as published
rows.note: Mongolia's 2020 census asked every citizen's ethnic group (үндэс угсаа). This is Table 3.2 of the National Statistics Office's English national report: the 3,174,565 Mongolian citizens it counted, by the census's own groups, with the counts as printed and each share taken from its count. 'Other ethnic groups' is the 143 people the table prints as other and the 2,364 people of the 6 groups too few to show at one decimal (Eljigen, Khamnigan, Tsaatan (Dukha), Uzbek (Chantuu), Kharchin and Khoshuud); 'Other nationals' are citizens of foreign origin. The base is citizens, so the 22,418 foreign nationals the census counted apart are outside it, as they are in the aimags' own shares (Appendix Table 3.6 of the same report). Being the country's own table, it stands in place of a sum of the aimags' shares, which that appendix prints to one decimal.

rows.source: Central Bureau of Statistics, DPR Korea, 2008 Population Census -- National Report (Pyongyang, 2009), Table 5: population by nationality, by 5-year age group and by sex
rows.license: Central Bureau of Statistics, DPR Korea. Official publication; copy served by the UN Statistics Division.
rows.note: North Korea's 2008 census asked nationality, not ethnicity: question P7, 'What is ____'s nationality?', answered Korean or Others. Table 5 of the National Report, the only table built from it, is national: 23,349,326 Koreans and 533 people of other nationalities, the 23,349,859 people the census counted in households and institutional living quarters (the 702,372 in military camps, which make the census's 24,052,231, were enumerated on a shorter form and are not in it). The 533 are 0.002% and too few to draw at one decimal. No table crosses nationality with a province, so the provinces carry the census's declaration instead.

rows.source: Sreda, Arena: Atlas of Religions and Nationalities of Russia (2012), arena_statistic.xls -- 'Распределение ответов в регионах РФ', column 'Население в целом'
rows.license: Sreda, published aggregate tabulation
rows.note: Sreda's Arena survey (fieldwork by the Public Opinion Foundation, MegaFOM omnibus, 29 May-25 June 2012, face to face at home): 56,900 adults aged 18 and over in 79 of the 83 federal subjects the map draws, 500 to 800 in each, which Sreda puts at 98.8% of the population -- Chechnya, Ingushetia, Chukotka and Nenets AO were not surveyed. Sreda's own figure for Russia as a whole, its subjects weighted by their populations; the counts are those weighted shares of the 56,900 respondents, not people. One answer from a card: 'Russian Orthodox Church' is 'I profess Orthodoxy and belong to the Russian Orthodox Church', 'Believe in God, no specific religion' is 'I believe in God (a higher power) but profess no particular religion', 'Atheist' is 'I do not believe in God'. A survey estimate, not a count: no Russian census since 1937 has asked religion. The subjects carry the same survey's own figures (russia_religion_survey.json).

groups.group: Not a member of any religious community
Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints

rows.source: Statistics Finland, table 11rx (population by religious community, age and sex), 31 December 2025
rows.license: CC BY 4.0 (Statistics Finland)
rows.note: Membership of a religious community as Finland's population register records it for every resident on 31 December 2025: 5,652,881 people (Statistics Finland, table 11rx). A count of registered membership, not of belief. 'Not a member of any religious community' is everyone in no registered community, which Statistics Finland calls no religious affiliation; it also holds people of faith who belong to none. 'Other Christian' joins the smaller Christian bodies the table names (Adventists, the Anglican churches, Baptists, the Lutheran free congregations, Methodists, the free churches and other Christians); 'Other religions' the Bahá'í, the Christian Community, the Liberal Catholic Church, the indigenous religions and neo-paganism and the rest of the other religious groups. Statistics Finland counts the communities apart for the whole country only: the regions and sub-regions carry the same register's three groups (the Lutheran church, every other community together, and none) for the same day, so this figure is the itemised whole of theirs.

rows.source: Statistics Committee of the Republic of Uzbekistan, Preliminary results of the Population and Agricultural Census of the Republic of Uzbekistan 2026 (Tashkent, 2026): population by nationality, and by region and native language

rows.note: Nationality as each person declared it in Uzbekistan's first census since 1989, taken at 15 January 2026: the preliminary results' national table, 39,047,321 people (the permanent population, the 2,090,953 temporarily away included). It is the exact sum of the fourteen regions the map draws, which carry the same table; the Factbook's estimate for the country, 37,015,151 for 2025, is 5.5% below the census's count. The preliminary results name seven nationalities and print the rest, 300,019 people, as 'other' (другие) without naming them; they replace the Factbook's older estimate. The final results are due by 1 July 2027.

rows.source: Bureau of National Statistics of Kazakhstan, 2021 National Population Census: National composition, religion and language proficiency in the Republic of Kazakhstan
rows.license: Official statistics of the Bureau of National Statistics; free to use with attribution
rows.note: The 2021 census asked each person's native language, and the Bureau of National Statistics publishes it for the republic only as whether the members of each nationality named their own nationality's language or another one, without saying which other (section 6 of National composition, religion and language proficiency in the Republic of Kazakhstan), so no language composition can be formed from it. Section 7 counts who can speak, read or write Kazakh, Russian and English, which is proficiency: one person may know all three. The Factbook's line for Kazakhstan -- Kazakh 80.1%, Russian 83.7%, English 35.1% (2021), 'based on population that understands the spoken language' -- is shares of that kind, 199% in all, and is not drawn as a composition; the regions and districts say the same.

The Factbook's line for Thailand -- Thai 97.5%, Burmese 1.3%, other 1.1%, unspecified under 0.1% (2015) -- counts nationality, as the Factbook's own note on it says. The provinces carry the share of Thai nationals that the 2000 census's provincial reports print; a sum of them would be a figure of 2000, so the country keeps this later one.
